en: He journeyed without turning back,
Went far, sparing no horse,
Traveled day after day and night after night.
Not lying down at night, he rode through the darkness.
He took no rest propped on his elbow,
Not even a brief nap.
He did not let Aktulpar stop to graze,
Nor lie down himself to sleep his fill.
Old Tashkent and Chaldybar—
The orphan descended and passed them.
The vast plain of Kazy-Kurt—
When he came to that open plain,
He saw the broad back of the earth.
There was no mountain even the size of a knucklebone,
No hollow to crouch down into.
On its hills were wild sheep,
On its terraces were ibex.
Snakes crawled down from the hills.
If you looked across its level plain,
Kulans without tails or manes,
Young two-year-olds ran and played.
The orphan could not tire of the sights.
Along the road his mother had fled,
The orphan traveled without wearying.
A salt-black desert, heaps of sand,
Not a blade of grass to nibble,
Not a drop of water to drink,
An empty plain, scorched sand—
The orphan traveled without wearying.
Kaiypchy's dark cave,
A true cave that was itself a shrine,
Where no one without ritual ablution stayed,
The wandering poor and destitute,
The gaunt one unable to find food,
We shall sell our coursers and pay tribute;
My poor mother Kanykei, weighed down by misery—
Gave protection like a father.
The widow took shelter and hid there.
Bakai came to her aid,
Roasted the meat of wild game.
The thin horse grew fat,
The hungry belly was filled.
Kaiypchy's dark cave where my mother had stayed—
Toward that dark cave he rode.
Aktulpar, the horse beneath him—
He let Aktulpar graze.
In Kaiypchy's cave
He lay down and slept his fill.
“My noble mother Kanykei,
When she scattered her wealth,
When my mother fled Talas on foot,
When she trotted like a hunting hound,
Enduring much hardship,
When my mother came on foot from Talas,
Her shoes worn out, walking in stockings,
Her precious life not extinguished by grief,
Her boots worn out, walking in stockings,
Her precious life not extinguished by humiliation,
Her calves chafed by walking,
My mother's heels aching,
Wishing to die but unable to die,
My dear mother, sorely tried,
Unable to take her own life,
Walking on foot toward Temir Khan,
When my mother set out wandering,
Fleeing on foot toward Bukhara,
Sobbing as she walked on foot—
This was where she entered, finding no other way.
My valiant mother Kanykei
Sheltered here for six days,
Stayed here to keep herself alive.
My poor mother Kanykei
Wore out her life, frail as a fly.
Weeping and wailing, my wretched mother
Prayed to God for me.
My poor, destitute mother's
Heart was sorely troubled:
“My orphan, left by the fierce-maned hero,
Will he die of hunger?” she thought.
The dark rock where she prayed—
Where her tears had fallen,
Currants sprouted green.
Where my mother had stood,
Oleaster fruit ripened in abundance.”
When he saw these signs,
The approaching orphan marveled.
His uncle Bakai, hastening anxiously,
Had come here seeking the orphan.
Six wild sheep and four wild rams—
Here his uncle had shot them for her.
He prepared all the provisions.
Honoring the spirit of dear Manas,
He sent her wandering to Temir Khan,
Sent her fleeing to Kara Khan,
Gave her two skins of milk,
Gave her two fat horses,
Lest she camp in an inhospitable place.
“When her husband dies, a woman
Finds her own kin close at hand,” he said.
Khan Bakai dedicated a gray two-year-old wether.
Here he slaughtered the animal as a sign.
My valiant mother Chyiyrdy
Lay here and ate her fill.
On the slope where the gray wether was slaughtered,
A shrine with a gray foundation arose.
My father, gone to Judgment Day,
God had thus protected.
Where my mother, burdened with hardship,
Had stayed the night,
A rooted shrine and a willow had sprung up.
That mighty conquering hero—
God had been his helper from the beginning.
Your orphan looked and wept in distress.
Whenever he saw one of those signs,
To his father Manas, the generous lord's
Spirit he prayed.
Unable to lie still, starting up,
Your orphan rose again
And saddled Aktulpar.
He traveled all around,
Along the road his mother had come,
The orphan wandered without wearying.
The gray pouch-belt left by his father Manas
He fitted closely about his neck.
To God, whose command is mighty,
Your orphan offered supplication and prayed.
He traveled toward Talas,
Went far without growing tired.
Ridges curved like saddle-bows—
He crossed many in succession.
Many hills and many ravines
He traversed without wearying.
He followed the path along their edges.
Oluya-Ata and the two Merki—
He traveled along them.
When he came to Oluya-Ata
And looked toward the sunset,
Kara-Balta and Sokuluk,
Their ridges showed dark in the distance.
When he could not see them, the orphan's
Heart was sorely troubled.
When he looked to his right,
A great, misty ridge
Rose curving like a valley.
When he saw that place,
The orphan gazing upon it
Felt his heart sorely troubled.
“My mother told me this:
When my mother fled Talas on foot,
That gray-mottled saddle, that broad valley—
That is the pass called Zhorgo.
When you cross over and descend,
There, on the other side, is Talas itself.”
Then the orphan thought:
“I shall cross that gray ridge,
Climb the saddle and look.”
So saying, Semetey
Crossed Zhorgo Pass.
Beyond lay Ken-Kol and Great Talas,
Where his father, who pledged himself to twelve spiritual masters,
The mighty Manas, had lived.
Looking down, he saw the green expanse:
The heart of Talas lay before him.
The orphan stood weeping,
Tears poured from his eyes,
His heart was sorely troubled.
His inheritance from his father,
Broad Talas, appeared before his eyes.
Zhylgynduu, Ken-Kol, Great Talas—
Was this not the broad back of the earth?
Would not a person dwelling here find peace?
Pass after separate pass appeared,
Places of exceptional joy appeared.
Ridge after hilly ridge appeared,
Many rolling stretches of land appeared.
Many separate upper valleys appeared,
Places like a special paradise appeared.
The great valley of broad Talas
Lay spreading wide,
Its valley sweeping in a broad curve.
Wild sheep poured down from the hills,
Thinning the grass on the hills.
Deer poured down from the rough ground,
Thinning the grass on the rough ground.
Ibex crowded upon the terraces.
Wild sheep's wool brushed against the crags.
Wild game gathered on the slopes,
Its male goats flocking by the hundred.
Wild sheep grazed upon the hills.
When the roe deer bounded down,
With its two arms stretched out,
Broad Talas lay there.
Its grass rose on towering stems.
When he breathed the scent of its sheltered hollows,
It smelled of paradise!
Its leaves were broad as leather.
My dear Talas's
Black widow spiders were thumb-sized.
It had marshes in separate patches,
Geese flying off in flocks.
Its pintails swayed in abundance.
Broad Talas lay there,
Red-headed ducks bobbing upon it.
Birds nested in the birches,
Flew as though driven by whips.
Birds nested in the plane trees,
Took wing with strength.
In its mountains were snowcocks.
Within its forests stood tranquil
Its splendidly grown plane trees.
To the lowlands of broad Talas,
Sparing nothing,
Almighty Allah, the one God,
Had granted all these things.
Entangled, unable to move through the grass,
They remained caught among it,
The young of stags and hinds.
“My Talas, left desolate!
He has departed from this world,
My fierce-maned father Manas!”
Within your orphan
Were many wounds that could not heal.
As he traveled farther,
There were many splendid sights.
The ground he crossed was rough.
Along a single troublesome path,
As the lone orphan traveled,
The slope down which he went was rugged:
The foothills of Uch-Koshoi.
Until death it will not be healed,
The bitterness of one who has suffered.
The hills stood separate, one by one.
When he had just reached the hills,
An inheritance left by his father Manas,
A white hunting hound appeared before his eyes.
From the rolling ridge
Something emerged, howling.
At that moment his plight was hard.
Unable to make it out, the orphan faltered.
Not recognizing Kumaik,
He wondered if it was a lion.
Its tongue hung down to the ground.
Its fur shimmered in three changing colors.
Unlike all other fanged beasts,
Unlike even a white tiger,
Was Kumaik's appearance.
As though he had seen the angel of death,
That orphan stood astonished.
Its form no mortal had ever seen;
It had a dragon's fearsome presence.
When it howled now and then,
Its voice was unlike any a human had heard.
Crouching through the foothills,
Kumaik came creeping low.
Tears welled in its eyes,
Kumaik came shedding them.
